Issued at 503 PM CDT Wed Aug 12 2026

-- FORECAST CHANGES OF NOTE/BIG PICTURE COMMENTS/UNCERTAINTIES:
- No truly major changes of note versus previous 7-day "forecast
  package", as summing things up in the shortest way possible: 
  We remain in a seasonably-active summer pattern, marked by 
  various/intermittent rain and thunderstorm chances 
  (occasionally severe), along with fairly typical temps by mid-
  August standards. 

- As for uncertainties, there are a few worth noting, ranging
  from very short term, to longer term:
1) Just how far south in our CWA will any severe storm threat
actually extend tonight? This forecaster continues to think that
SPC is probably at least 1-2 counties too generously south with
its official Slight Risk (level 2 of 5 area), as various high-
res models are fairly insistent that the MAIN threat area should
be MAINLY north of I-80. 

2) In the longer term, am not overly-comfortable with Saturday
night currently sporting such high rain chances/PoPs (mainly 
60-70%) that far out in time, but at least for now, "on paper"
this appears to be one of the better chances for much of our CWA
(not just parts of it) to pick up some decent rain. 

3) Our official high temperature forecast calls for much of our
area (mainly Nebraska) only reaching the 70s Sunday-Monday.
However, am thinking we might be aiming a little TOO cool here,
as latest set of model guidance suggests 80s are probably more
likely (unless of course it ends up being particularly
cloudy/rainy. 


-- 7-DAY FORECAST CHRONOLOGICAL RUNDOWN (through Wed. Aug. 19):
- CURRENT/RECENT WEATHER SCENE AS OF 4 PM:
Not that we've heard ANY complaints, but except for perhaps our
far southern counties in KS, high temps are on track to
"underachieve" by a few-to-several degrees versus earlier
forecasts, as fairly widespread coverage of mid-level clouds and
a smattering of high-based showers/weak thunderstorms (most weak
storms were this morning) have continue to percolate over our
CWA. As a result, actual high temps are on track to "only" top
out a few degrees either side of 90 in most of our CWA, with any
mid-upper 90s to perhaps low-100s confined to mainly our KS
counties (particularly our "bottom three"). Directly related to
this, heat index readings have also been held down somewhat,
with any 100-105+ values mostly confined to our KS counties
along with the Furnas County area. Will let the previously-
issued Heat Advisory "ride" through 9 PM for all 6 of our KS
counties, but in reality only parts of our bottom three
(Rooks/Osborne/Mitchell) probably stand a chance of reaching
official criteria of 105+. 

In the big picture aloft, water vapor satellite imagery and 
short term model data confirm that our area resides under
generally west-southwesterly flow aloft, as we reside in the
proverbial "ring of fire" zone along the northern periphery of a
ridge/high pressure centered mainly over OK/TX. At the surface,
the vast majority of our CWA resides north of a rather sharp,
west-east oriented quasi-stationary front that lies across
northern KS. To the north of this boundary, easterly breezes
generally 10-15 MPH prevail, while to the south of this front
(which does clip at least southern parts of
Rooks/Osborne/Mitchell counties in our far south,more southerly
breezes prevail with temperatures 100+ degrees. 


- THIS EVENING-OVERNIGHT:
By FAR the main concern is a chance for a complex/cluster of
strong to perhaps severe storms to track across mainly the
northern 1/3rd of our CWA mainly between 11 PM-5 AM. Leaning
heavily on latest higher-res models such as HRRR/RRFS, while
some very spotty high-based showers could continue into early
evening mainly in our southern counties (near/south of the KS
border), at least the vast majority of our CWA should remain
dry/thunderstorm-free until at least 11 PM (prior to this,
initially more isolated strong/severe storms currently
developing out near the NE/WY/CO border area will gradually grow
"upscale" into a larger complex as it approaches our CWA). Once
storms arrive (again, MOST favored north of I-80 but with at
least spotty/isolated activity perhaps as far south as near the
state line), the "million dollar question" is how severe they
might be? While deep-layer shear will be fairly modest (mainly
around 35KT or less), the presence of at least 1000-2000 J/kg
instability/CAPE and convergence along the nose/exit region of a
somewhat strong southerly low level jet (LLJ) will surely give
storms a chance to provide somewhat of a punch, especially IF
they are able to maintain a notable cold pool/outflow surge. Of
greatest concern are potential wind gusts up to ~ 65 MPH, with a
lesser threat of hail up to around quarter size. A few places
could get a quick 1-2" of rain, but fairly progressive motion of
the complex should limit flooding potential. By around 5 AM, the
main complex should be fairly cleanly departed east of our CWA,
